analysis.one_liner: Grants part-time workers family leave, 401(k) access, and equal treatment with full-time coworkers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died with 22 Democratic cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal rules so part-time workers are treated more like full-time workers. It would let employees qualify for family and medical leave after 12 months on the job without a minimum-hours test, require employers to let long-term part-timers join 401(k)-type plans after two years of at least 500 hours each, and bar employers with more than 15 workers from paying part-timers less or giving them worse schedules, benefits, and promotion chances when they do substantially the same work. It would also require employers to offer available extra hours to existing part-time employees before hiring new people, with penalties and a private right of action to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time workers — roughly a quarter of the U.S. workforce, disproportionately women, caregivers, students, and older workers — would gain access to unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave that currently requires a 1,250-hour work history, and to employer 401(k) plans after two years of at least 500 hours. Part-timers doing substantially equal work would have to be paid and scheduled on comparable terms with full-timers, and could sue to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Part-time workers, mostly women and caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 12-month/1,250-hour work-history test from the Family and Medical Leave Act, so a part-time employee with 12 months on the job qualifies for family and medical leave [S2][S3].

Caps employer service requirements for 401(k) and 403(b) plan participation at two consecutive 12-month periods of at least 500 hours for workers 21 and over, with a $10,000-per-employee-per-year penalty on plans that refuse [S2][S3].

Prohibits employers with more than 15 employees from giving part-timers lower pay, less notice of schedules, pro-rated benefits, or weaker promotion opportunities for substantially equal work, and requires them to offer available additional hours to existing employees before hiring outsiders [S2][S3].
Gives workers a private right of action with double (liquidated) damages, attorney's fees, and Labor Department enforcement to back the new rights [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely heavily on part-time labor — retail, restaurants, hospitality, staffing agencies, and franchise chains — would bear the costs: equalized pay and benefits, retirement plan coverage for long-term part-timers, paid make-whole compensation when they fill hours with new hires instead of existing employees, and three years of compliance recordkeeping.

drawbacks.text: The offer-of-hours rule requires employers to pay existing employees for hours worked by a new hire if the existing employee wanted those hours, which adds payroll costs and constrains how employers fill shifts and use temporary or contract labor [S3].

Equal pay and pro-rated benefits for substantially equal work would raise labor costs for employers that staff heavily with part-timers, and some good-faith supporters acknowledge this could reduce the number of part-time positions or lead employers to consolidate hours into fewer full-time jobs — an outcome that helps some workers and eliminates schedules others want.

The compliance burden is real: employers must collect and update written statements of each employee's desired hours and availability, document every offer of additional hours and response, and keep those records for at least three years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver genuine gains to a large, historically under-protected group — access to family leave and retirement savings that full-time workers take for granted, and a legal right to equal treatment. The trade-off is higher and more complicated scheduling and benefits administration for part-time-reliant employers, and some risk that employers respond by cutting part-time openings or converting them into fewer full-time jobs, which would not help workers who specifically want limited hours. The enforcement design (double damages, fees, private lawsuits) is strong, which helps workers but increases litigation exposure for employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act on February 9, 2022, with 10 original Democratic cosponsors [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the Education and Labor, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Ways and Means Committees; that referral is the last action in the bill's history [S5].
The bill finished the Congress with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the action history, and no vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that depend on part-time labor — retail, restaurant, hospitality, and staffing firms — are better off, because they avoided the equal-treatment, leave, and retirement-coverage requirements without ever having to argue against them on the record.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 22 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. DeLauro, Pressley, Porter, Jayapal, and Doggett
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of its support came from Republicans.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, and House Administration Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the portions of the bill within their jurisdictions.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican ever signed on, but no member or group ever had to vote on the bill or publicly oppose it, so the opposition never shows up in the record.

industries.note: These businesses staff heavily with part-timers and often pay them less and give them weaker schedules and benefits for similar work. The bill would require equal treatment, pro-rated benefits, and first offers of extra hours to existing staff, raising their labor costs.

The bill bars employers from hiring through temp or staffing agencies to fill hours that existing part-time employees have said they want, cutting off a channel these firms rely on. Franchise chains would also be covered as integrated enterprises.

Plans could not keep long-term part-timers out beyond two 500-hour years, and would face a $10,000-per-employee annual penalty for excluding them. Plan sponsors and recordkeepers would absorb added coverage and administrative costs, though employers may exclude such workers from certain nondiscrimination tests.
